result.summary: Mercury finishes lulling the hundred-eyed Argus to sleep and kills him with his sword, throwing his body from the rock. Juno takes his eyes and sets them in the tail of her peacock.

scenes.title: Death of Argus
scenes.summary: Mercury sees all of Argus's eyes asleep, stops his tale, seals the sleep with his wand and beheads him. Juno then puts the eyes on her peacock's tail.
scenes.stakes: Argus loses his life when he falls asleep on guard; Io's captivity depends on his watch.

place.name: the rock where Argus kept watch

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet from Mount Cyllene, his birthplace in Arcadia.

notable_quotes.reason: Ovid's apostrophe to the dead Argus, with the striking image of one night taking a hundred eyes.

analysis.text: The passage ends Argus's watch over Io through cunning rather than force, and it also explains why the peacock's tail has eyes, as many Metamorphoses stories explain a natural feature.
The peacock was associated with Juno in Greek and Roman tradition, and Ovid links that association to Argus's eyes.

legacy.text: The image of Argus's eyes on the peacock's tail became a common motif in later European art and literature.

fun_facts.text: Mercury's epithet Cyllenian comes from Mount Cyllene in Arcadia, where he was said to have been born.

language_notes.text: "Cyllenian God" is Mercury, named for Mount Cyllene in Arcadia, where he was said to have been born.
"Languid" means drooping or weary; here it describes eyes heavy with sleep.
"Crooked sword" translates a curved blade (harpe), a sickle-like weapon also associated with Perseus.
"Daughter of Saturn" is Juno. Her bird is the peacock, and its tail's eye-spots are explained as Argus's eyes.

context_notes.text: Mercury's wand (caduceus) has the power to bring sleep. He uses it to make sure Argus's eyes stay shut.
Juno had set Argus to guard Io, whom Jove had turned into a heifer. Argus's death frees Io from this watch.

literary_notes.text: The narrator turns to address the dead Argus directly, adding pathos and a sense of mourning to the killing.
Death is presented as a single night closing over a hundred eyes, contrasting the many lights with one darkness.
The peacock's tail spots are called "starry gems", turning the eyes into jewels and giving the bird's pattern a mythic origin.
